title: The Coming Patent Storm in AI Hardware
content:
Firm Events
District Court vs. PTAB: Strategic Forum Selection in Life Sciences Patent Disputes
December 10, 2026 | 12:00 PM – 1:00 PM ET
The global semiconductor industry reached record sales of $795.6 billion in 2025, according to the Semiconductor Industry Association’s “2026 State of the U.S. Semiconductor Industry” report, with AI chips now driving roughly half of total revenue while representing less than 0.2% of total unit volume. That concentration of value in a small number of advanced devices is the kind of condition that tends to drive patent assertion. When billions of dollars of revenue flow through technology that only a handful of companies produce, and every producer must solve the same underlying engineering problems, patent rights over those solutions become valuable enough to fight over.
Three structural forces are now converging to make AI-specific semiconductor hardware the next major front in patent litigation: (1) the sheer scale of capital being invested in AI infrastructure; (2) a set of well-defined physical and engineering bottlenecks that every competitor must overcome; and (3) a patent landscape that is reaching maturity across all of the relevant technology areas simultaneously.
The first major front is already open. The fundamental constraint on AI accelerator performance is not compute; it is memory bandwidth. Graphics processing unit (GPU) compute density has scaled far faster than memory bandwidth, leaving even the most powerful AI accelerators starved of data. The industry’s solution, high-bandwidth memory (HBM), stacks dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) dies vertically using through-silicon vias (TSVs) directly atop or beside the GPU die, delivering bandwidth measured in terabytes per second. HBM is no longer optional; it is now standard architecture in every leading AI accelerator in production today.
The economics of this market make litigation likely. The HBM market was valued at $2.93 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach $16.72 billion by 2033, growing at a 21.35% compound annual growth rate driven almost entirely by generative AI demand, according to Patsnap. HBM demand grew 130% year-over-year in 2025, and global HBM spend is projected to grow 58% year over year in 2026 to reach $54.6 billion, approaching $100 billion by 2028, a figure that would surpass the size of the entire 2024 DRAM market, according to Global X ETFs.
The supply side is equally concentrated. SK Hynix holds approximately 50% to 62% of the HBM market (depending on report date), Micron approximately 18% to 21%, and Samsung approximately 17% to 33%. That concentrated supply structure means a single valid patent on TSV stacking, base die design, or HBM controller architecture could reach nearly every AI accelerator shipped worldwide.
The litigation has already begun. DRAM patent disputes rose 119% in U.S. district courts in 2025, with NAND disputes up 56% year over year. In May 2026, a Texas-based technology company filed patent infringement actions in the the Eastern and Western Districts of Texas, the District of Delaware, and the International Trade Commission (ITC) targeting Nvidia, SK Hynix, Kioxia, Corsair, and Western Digital, asserting patents directed at memory technologies, as reported by Law360.
The ITC presents distinct strategic advantages for semiconductor patent disputes that explain why sophisticated patent holders increasingly file parallel actions there. Unlike district court litigation, ITC investigations proceed on a statutory 15-to-18-month timeline, delivering a final determination before most district court cases reach claim construction. The remedy — an exclusion order barring infringing products from entering the U.S. — can be devastating for companies dependent on global supply chains, particularly when the targeted component is manufactured exclusively overseas, as HBM and advanced packaging substrates largely are. For patent holders, even the credible threat of an exclusion order can accelerate settlement negotiations that would otherwise stall in district court. For respondents, ITC proceedings demand immediate resource allocation; the accelerated discovery schedule and limited opportunities for stays leave little room for delay. Companies with significant import exposure should assess their ITC risk profile now, particularly for products incorporating HBM, advanced packaging, or CPO components sourced from Asian fabs. For more on ITC practice, see Troutman Pepper Locke’s The Top Five Challenges of Pursuing Litigation at the ITC.
The second major front involves the architecture that allows modern AI accelerators to be built at all. No single silicon die can integrate all the logic, memory, and I/O functions needed for a frontier AI processor; reticle size limits and fabrication yield economics make monolithic design increasingly unviable. The industry has converged on a “chiplet” model: distinct compute, memory, and I/O dies fabricated separately and joined at the package level, through silicon interposer wafers, which are then mounted onto a larger organic substrate. The critical question, and the patent battleground, is how those dies communicate.
Three interconnect families are racing to become the industry standard: UCIe (Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express), CXL (Compute Express Link), and NVLink. Patent filings in this space are heavy and increasingly contentious. For example, multiple assignees, including Intel, Shanghai QuXin, and others, filed patents in 2025 and 2026 proposing to route UCIe signals directly over organic package substrates to connect compute dies with HBM stacks, bypassing expensive silicon interposers entirely, according to Patsnap’s UCIe patent landscape. If organic-substrate HBM routing becomes a common implementation path for UCIe-compliant chiplet designs, patents covering it could function similarly to standard-essential patents, with licensing/FRAND implications for anyone building UCIe-compliant AI accelerators.
Companies participating in standard-setting bodies carry patent disclosure obligations, and failing to manage them carefully can create real legal exposure. Companies that have not yet audited their portfolio against pending standard specifications should do so promptly. For companies that are implementers rather than contributors, the FRAND licensing framework provides a degree of protection, but only if the implementer understands which patents in a licensor’s portfolio are genuinely essential and which are merely declared. Engaging patent counsel to conduct SEP essentiality analysis before entering licensing negotiations is a necessary step that is routinely deferred until after the first demand letter arrives. On the other hand, companies looking to monetize or assert their patent assets should map their interconnect portfolios against industry standards and specifications such as UCIe.
The third, and arguably most consequential, front over the next five years involves the replacement of copper electrical interconnects with optical ones at the chip-package level. Traditional copper traces between a switch application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) and its optical transceivers are reaching fundamental physical limits. At 800G and 1.6T data rates, signal loss in the electrical traces becomes severe enough to limit system performance and efficiency. Co-packaged optics (CPO) addresses this by integrating the optical engine directly onto the same package as the switch ASIC, eliminating the electrical bottleneck entirely. CPO is a key enabler for AI and data center scale-up as noted at Nvidia’s GTC 2025 conference.
The capital flowing into this space is substantial. The global silicon photonics and CPO market was valued at $2.16 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $22.4 billion by 2034, at a compound annual growth rate of 29.5%, according to this report. report.summary: Explosive AI chip revenue, a memory-bandwidth bottleneck, the chiplet interconnect race and co-packaged optics are converging to trigger a wave of semiconductor patent litigation.
report.background: The global semiconductor industry posted record sales of $795.6 billion in 2025, with AI chips driving roughly half of total revenue while accounting for less than 0.2% of unit volume. That extreme value concentration — billions of dollars flowing through technology only a handful of firms can produce — is exactly the condition that historically precedes patent assertion. For years, semiconductor IP disputes were dampened by broad cross-licenses among vertically integrated giants and long product cycles. That equilibrium is now under strain: AI infrastructure capital has exploded, new entrants and non-practicing entities have entered the market, and patent portfolios across high-bandwidth memory, chiplet interconnects and co-packaged optics are maturing simultaneously. Three structural forces — capital scale, shared engineering bottlenecks every competitor must solve the same way, and a patent landscape maturing across all relevant technology areas at once — make AI-specific hardware the next major litigation front.

report.impact: For the AI industry, the shift from cross-licensing détente to active assertion raises the cost and risk of every new accelerator program. Expect more defensive portfolios, patent-pool and FRAND negotiations, deeper IP due diligence in M&A, and pressure to localize manufacturing to avoid ITC exclusion orders. For developers, chiplet-based startups and anyone building UCIe-compliant silicon face licensing exposure they may not have budgeted for; hardware teams should treat freedom-to-operate analysis as a design input, not an afterthought. For regular users, the downstream effects are subtler but real: licensing costs feed into accelerator pricing, exclusion orders can tighten supply of specific parts, and litigation uncertainty may slow the rollout of next-generation data-center capacity that cloud and AI services depend on.
report.tools: To follow the patent landscape, use Google Patents and the USPTO Patent Public Search for full-text and assignment data, Espacenet for global families, and Lens.org or PatSnap for citation and landscape analytics; PatentsView offers a free API for bulk analysis. Track ITC complaints through the EDIS database. For standards exposure, read the UCIe and CXL Consortium specifications directly and monitor declarations of essentiality. Open-source projects mapping SEP declarations are limited, so most serious work still requires counsel-led essentiality analysis.
